A good example of this is the demytholog: A good example of this is the demythologizing of the battle before creation in Genesis 1.
A number of passages suggest that certai: A number of passages suggest that certain “signs” or preliminary phenomena may indicate that Jesus’s parousia or other parousia events are imminent (Matt 24:4-34; Mark 13:5-20; Luke 21:8-28; 2Thess 2:1-12; 1John 2:18). Other texts call on readers to be ready because such events will take place without warning (see, e.g., Matt 24:43-44).
According to (2Sam 21:19), however, Goli: According to (2Sam 21:19), however, Goliath was defeated by Elhanan, one of David’s warriors. Some interpreters have suggested that the name of the Philistine slain by David was not given in the original, oldest tradition and that the name of Elhanan’s victim was substituted for the anonymous adversary of the better-known David.
According to Genesis 1:1–2:4a (the p acc: According to Genesis 1:1–2:4a (the p account according to the documentary hypothesis), God created the world in six days and rested on the seventh day.
According to the J source, in Genesis 4:: According to the J source, in Genesis 4:26, the earliest humans worshiped Yahweh as Yahweh.
Although some scholars suggest that “unn: Although some scholars suggest that “unnatural” (Greek para physin) relations concerns birth control or nonprocreative heterosexual intercourse, the context suggests that Paul is talking about same-sex sexual relationships between women (Rom 1:26).
Although this vision of the end claims t: Although this vision of the end claims to happen during the Babylonian exile, circa 546 B.C.E. (Daniel 8:1), the passage itself was written in or near Jerusalem around 167 B.C.E., during the Hellenistic period.
Ananda Geyser-Fouché and Ebele Chukwuka': Ananda Geyser-Fouché and Ebele Chukwuka's article in HTS Teologiese Studies calls 1 Chronicles 21 a much-debated text, primarily because of the presence of Satan or satan. It reports that some scholars see the figure as an attempt to remove evil from Yahweh, and that English translations follow a long tradition of reading Satan as a proper noun; the authors conclude that Satan there still serves as a common noun for an adversary, and that Chronicles holds evil as well as good to come from God. Adam Porter's Bible Odyssey article says 1 Chronicles 21:1 is the only place the Hebrew Bible uses the noun as a name. The Encyclopaedia Judaica says the article is dropped there and Satan seems to be a real proper name, substituted for “the Lord” because of doctrinal considerations. W. F. Barnett's entry in the New Catholic Encyclopedia reads the verse as showing that the Chronicler knew a personal principle of evil that warred against God.
And the rejection of this motif or this: And the rejection of this motif or this idea in Genesis 1 is pointed and purposeful.
Andrew Perrin lists Daniel 2:4b–7:28 amo: Andrew Perrin lists Daniel 2:4b–7:28 among the biblical texts composed in Aramaic. Daniel Smith-Christopher names the two languages as the first of the book's problems, alongside its two kinds of literature. The publisher's summary of Coogan and Chapman's introduction says the Aramaic sections suggest that the text may be a composite. H. J. M. van Deventer says the two languages do not correspond with the two literary types, court tales and visions, a problem he counts among those scholars have not yet been able to solve.
Another story of creation, Genesis 2:4b–: Another story of creation, Genesis 2:4b–24 (the j account according to the documentary hypothesis)
As we have already seen in Exodus 12.37,: As we have already seen in Exodus 12.37, the biblical writers often inflated census statistics; therefore it is not surprising that the population statistics found in Numbers are also unrealistically high.
Benjamin Sommer's Bible Odyssey article: Benjamin Sommer's Bible Odyssey article says some of the latest texts of the Hebrew Bible start using names for angels, such as Gabriel and Michael in Daniel, written in the second century BCE. Amy Merrill Willis's Bible Odyssey article says Daniel provides the first references to Michael and Gabriel as named angels. Bernard Bamberger's entry in the Encyclopaedia Judaica says that in Daniel the angels now have proper names, that it is the only biblical book in which angels have distinct personalities, and that it is the first in which each nation has an angelic patron. Gershom Scholem's entry says Raphael first appears as an angel's name in Tobit 12:15 and 1 Enoch 20:3, where he is one of the seven archangels, and Joshua Gutmann's says later apocalyptic writings name Uriel and others as interpreters of visions. Sommer says that by Daniel's time polytheism was no longer a major threat, so authors could speak of heavenly beings more freely; Gutmann says the conditions for a special doctrine of angels existed only in the Hellenistic period.

Benjamin Sommer's Bible Odyssey article says the Hebrew mal'akh, like the Greek angelos, means “messenger”; the Hebrew Bible occasionally uses it of a human messenger, but typically of heavenly beings who serve Yhwh. Stephen White's article in the Tyndale Bulletin says the word means messenger or representative, both human and divine. The Encyclopaedia Judaica's entry by Bernard Bamberger says the term is frequently applied to human agents, that the Greek angelos has the same range of meanings, and that the word took on the exclusive meaning “angel” only when it passed through Latin into other European languages; it also says the angel is often called simply “man”. T. L. Fallon's entry in the New Catholic Encyclopedia says angels sent by God appeared for the most part in human form, and that only one angel in the Bible is said to be able to fly (Daniel 9:21).
Beyond these sources found in 1 Samuel,: Beyond these sources found in 1 Samuel, 2 Samuel 9–20 and 1 Kings 1–2 primarily draw from another hypothetical source called the “Succession Narrative.” This source is so named because it presumably was composed as an explanation of how and why Solomon became David’s heir.
Books associated with Enoch were popular: Books associated with Enoch were popular among ancient Christians, and a selection from the Book of the Watchers (which we find today in 1 Enoch) is quoted in Jude 14-15. Many scholars also think that 2Pet 2:4 and Jude 6 allude to the punishment of fallen angels described in literature connected to Enoch.
Breed writes that scholars think many of: Breed writes that scholars think many of the Old Greek translators worked from early Hebrew versions of biblical books that were quite different from those that became the Masoretic Text, and that discoveries in the Dead Sea region show these alternate Hebrew versions circulated alongside the versions that became the Masoretic Text. When the Greek translation was made, he adds, there was no Masoretic Text or any official Bible, only multiple editions of many scrolls. Samuel Thomas's Bible Odyssey answer agrees that in some cases the Hebrew text behind the Septuagint was clearly different from, and perhaps earlier than, the Masoretic Text, and points to certain manuscripts among the Dead Sea Scrolls. Davies's Encyclopaedia Judaica entry reports Qumran manuscripts of Isaiah that support Septuagint readings and Hebrew copies of the shorter edition of Jeremiah known from the Septuagint. Translators also made choices of their own. Discussing how the Greek renders the Hebrew word ‘almah, Thomas cautions that it is sometimes difficult to say why a particular scribe or translator made a particular decision, and notes that in Isaiah 7:14 the translator had several choices for translation.
Breed writes that until the last few dec: Breed writes that until the last few decades most biblical scholars believed the Masoretic texts were, with some exceptions, the best witnesses to the most ancient Hebrew text, and that the Dead Sea Scrolls have since suggested several different versions of many books. Thomas writes that recent gains in textual criticism mean we can no longer say whether the Septuagint or the Masoretic Text represents a more original text, if such a thing can even be spoken of, at least in the case he discusses, Psalm 16:10. Davies's entry says that in a few cases a Qumran reading is clearly superior to the Masoretic Text; his example is Deuteronomy 32:8, where a Qumran manuscript agrees with the Septuagint against the Masoretic Text.
But the prohibition is against male prac: But the prohibition is against male practice, not female, a fact that has led commentators to argue that the (likely male) authors were fixated on male nonprocreative intercourse (compare the “spilling of seed” by Onan in Gen 38:9-10).
By this view, the reason for “seven clea: By this view, the reason for “seven clean” animals in one tradition is that Noah will offer a sacrifice following the flood (Gen 8:20), whereas in the other tradition, which is often associated with priestly interests in ancient Israel, no such sacrifice will be offered since sacrifice is the exclusive domain of priests.
Carol Meyers's Bible Odyssey article say: Carol Meyers's Bible Odyssey article says close study revealed biblical narratives to be replete with inconsistencies and even outright contradictions: in 1 Samuel 17:50 David kills Goliath, but in 2 Samuel 21:19 Elhanan does, and Joshua says the Israelites conquered the whole land while Judges describes the survival of many Canaanites; Hayes's lecture on Joshua and Judges adds that Judges 1 gives a long list of the places from which the Canaanites were not expelled. Hayes's lectures say the Bible contains a lot of repetition and contradiction, and that its legal materials contradict one another. The chapter summary for Coogan and Chapman's textbook says almost all biblical scholars explain the Pentateuch's repetitions, inconsistencies and contradictions by distinct sources from different historical periods. Chronicles retells Samuel and Kings: Hayes calls it the Bible interpreting itself, the textbook summary says its David has several substantive differences from the earlier account, and Jesse Ainslie and Joseph Lam's Bible Odyssey article says Kings and Chronicles tell two very different stories about King Manasseh.
Christine Hayes reports that most agree: Christine Hayes reports that most agree the oldest account of the event at the sea is a poetic fragment in Exodus 15:1–12. The notes of the New American Bible say that many scholars regard the poem (15:1–21) as one of the oldest compositions in the Bible, and that it was once an independent work. The Encyclopaedia Judaica's article on Exodus finds several early features in its language, but judges that its mentions of Philistia, cavalry and the sanctuary on God's mountain put the present form of the song no earlier than the tenth century BCE.
Christine Hayes says Belshazzar was neve: Christine Hayes says Belshazzar was never king but a prince regent, defeated by Cyrus, not Darius, that the Median king Darius is unknown to history, and that these inaccuracies are a sign of a much later writer looking back. Amy Merrill Willis counts Daniel's seventy-year career under Babylonian, Median and Persian kings among the book's historical difficulties, and says Nebuchadnezzar's exile in chapter 4 may have been based on Nabonidus, adding that an account outside the Bible has Nabonidus consulting a Jewish seer. Daniel Smith-Christopher and Lawrence Wills note that a story called the Prayer of Nabonidus, found among the Dead Sea Scrolls, resembles the tales of Daniel 1–6.
Christine Hayes's Yale lecture says ther: Christine Hayes's Yale lecture says there are in fact two creation stories in Genesis, with quite a few contradictions between them: the first, in Genesis 1, concludes in Genesis 2:4, and the second begins in Genesis 2:4 and runs into Genesis 3. The chapter summary for Coogan and Chapman's introductory textbook likewise says Genesis provides two distinct creation myths, the first in 1:1–2:4a and the second in 2:4b–3:24, and that their differences suggest the accounts were written by two authors. In the Documentary Hypothesis the first account is attributed to P, the Priestly source, and the second to J, which Hayes says begins with the second creation story, in the second half of Genesis 2:4; the notes of the New American Bible, Revised Edition (NABRE) also assign Genesis 1:1–2:3 to the Priestly source. Shalom Paul's Encyclopaedia Judaica entry calls them the P and J accounts according to the documentary hypothesis and says their sources reflect different epic traditions. The textbook summary for the next chapter adds that, although the evidence does not fit the classical form of the hypothesis as neatly as scholars once thought, almost all biblical scholars recognize that the Pentateuch's repetitions, inconsistencies and contradictions are best explained by distinct sources from different periods.
Christine Hayes's Yale lectures say that: Christine Hayes's Yale lectures say that although many later Hellenistic Jewish texts and the New Testament identify the snake as a Satan, in Genesis 3 it is simply a talking animal. Brad Anderson's Bible Odyssey article says the text does not reveal the serpent's nature or identity, that the serpent's association with evil became common in Judaism in the Second Temple period (1 Enoch, the Life of Adam and Eve), and that it was not a long stretch for readers to equate it with Satan. The New American Bible calls Wisdom 2:24 the first biblical text to equate the serpent of Genesis 3 with the devil, and says Christian tradition identified the snake with the devil, citing also John 8:44 and Revelation 12:9 and 20:2. Shawna Dolansky's Bible Odyssey talk says biblical scholars think the “ancient serpent” of Revelation is the serpent of the ancient Near Eastern combat myth, and that the associations of Satan are not brought together with the serpent in the garden until early Christian writings.
Christine Hayes's Yale lectures say the: Christine Hayes's Yale lectures say the outcry God hears is against the Sodomites' violation of the law of hospitality to strangers and their desire to gang rape them, and that the idea that Sodom's fundamental sin was homosexual behavior is not present in the Hebrew Bible but appears only in later documents. J. Stiebert's article in Verbum et Ecclesia says what is at issue is primarily gang rape and the humiliation of male visitors, in Genesis 19 and the similar story in Judges 19, and reads Ezekiel 16:49 as condemning Sodom for pride, social injustice and lack of hospitality. Jan Joosten's article in the Journal of Theological Studies says the projected sex is condemned because it was not consensual. Rhiannon Graybill's Bible Odyssey article on Judges 19 says the focus is on the failure to show hospitality, with rape threats used to establish dominance over male foreigners. Eoghan Ahern's article in the Journal of the History of Sexuality says studies have shown the homosexual reading of Sodom was an addition of later commentators. The HarperCollins Bible Dictionary records both attempted sexual perversity and gross inhospitality in the story. Cephas Tushima's article in Old Testament Essays notes that others continue to hold the traditional view, and reads Lot's offer of his daughters as a response to the idea of men having sex with men.
Close study of biblical narratives revea: Close study of biblical narratives revealed that they are replete with inconsistencies and even outright contradictions. For example, humans are created before vegetation in Gen 2:4-9 but afterward in Gen 1:11-27. Or in 1Sam 17:50, David kills Goliath, whereas in 2Sam 21:19, Elhanan does.
Dale Martin's Yale lectures say some rea: Dale Martin's Yale lectures say some readers take Romans 1 as a condemnation of modern homosexuality and believe that is a sound historical reading, while others, using the same historical-critical methods, say homosexuality is not Paul's concern. William Loader's HTS article reports that Robert Gagnon, as do many in current debates, distinguishes homosexual orientation from the act and argues that Paul's focus is the act. Bruce Wells calls Gagnon's 2001 book the older, more conservative view and says the more progressive views of Jennifer Knust's and Michael Coogan's books are accepted by most academic scholars today.
Devil: the first biblical text to equate: Devil: the first biblical text to equate the serpent of Gn 3 with the devil.
Early LGBTQ+ interpretation focused prim: Early LGBTQ+ interpretation focused primarily on challenging heterosexist and cis-normative readings of a collection of biblical passages commonly called the “clobber passages” (e.g., Gen 19:1–11; Lev 18:22; 20:13; Rom 1:26–28; 1 Cor 6:9–10; 1 Tim 1:9–10).
Enuma Elish, the Babylonian creation epi: Enuma Elish, the Babylonian creation epic, tells how the god Marduk defeats Tiamat, the primeval salt-water ocean, and builds the world from her carcass. Kacie Klamm's Bible Odyssey article says it was likely composed in the second millennium BCE, long before the earliest parts of the Bible were written down. Hayes points to the resemblances: Genesis 1 opens with a temporal clause, as the epic does, has a wind sweep over chaotic waters as Marduk's wind was released into the face of Tiamat, and has God set up the heavenly bodies, as Marduk did. Klamm adds that Genesis 1 runs over seven days and the epic over seven tablets, and that humans are made on the sixth day and in the sixth tablet. Paul's entry finds the same sequence of events in both, firmament, dry land, luminaries, humans and divine rest, and concludes that at least the P account appears to echo the earlier Babylonian story. The Coogan and Chapman summary likewise says Enuma Elish shares a number of affinities with Genesis 1. There are differences too. In Genesis, Hayes says, there is no battle: a listener who knew the old story would hear the wind and the watery deep, and then only a word, “let there be light”. Hayes and the Coogan and Chapman summary describe Genesis 1 as demythologizing the older material; Paul writes that Genesis totally rejects mythology and that the differences are much more striking than the similarities. In Enuma Elish, Hayes says, service was imposed on humans so that the gods were free; in Genesis 1 the creation of humans is the climactic act, and they are given rule over the other creatures. Klamm reports that scholars explain the similarities differently: some biblical writers may have known the epic, given Babylon's power, while others think both texts drew on common ancient Near Eastern beliefs.
Exodus 6:2-4, a very important passage,: Exodus 6:2-4, a very important passage, is assigned to P, and here God says, "I am [Yahweh]. I appeared to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob as El Shaddai, but I did not make Myself known to them by My name [Yahweh]."
Extra-biblical records and accounts sugg: Extra-biblical records and accounts suggest that some materials from the first half of the book of Daniel may be based on Neo-Babylonian realities. Notably, Nebuchadnezzar’s exile (Dan 4) may have been based on the Neo-Babylonian king Nabonidus. There is even an extra-biblical account of Nabonidus consulting with a Jewish seer, as Nebuchadnezzar does in chapter 4. Yet the extra-biblical account does not name Daniel.
Finkelstein calls the great united monar: Finkelstein calls the great united monarchy a literary construct of late-monarchic Judahite authors, and Brian Schmidt's summary of his argument ties it to a later Josianic ideal of uniting the two states under Jerusalem. Sergi says political unity between Israel and Judah could only be imagined after Israel fell in 720 BCE. Nakhai says some scholars read the Bible's united kingdom as an elegy to a long-lost national unity, and the Encyclopaedia Judaica's history entry that the biblical writers sometimes projected the events and institutions of their own time onto earlier times. Nadav Na'aman says most scholars of Israel's early history have treated the account of David's conquests in 2 Samuel 8 as late historiography that does not reflect the ancient reality, and himself supports the view that David's conquests there were modelled on the victories of foreign kings. On what lies behind the picture, Finkelstein suggests the seed may have been Jerusalem's chiefs taking over the former Saulide territories, and Schmidt reports his view that if any Israelite kingdom ever united north and south, it was the Omride kingdom ruled from Samaria in the ninth century; Sergi roots the idea of unity under David in the actual unity of Judah and Benjamin under the house of David in the early Iron IIA. Mazar holds that parts of the account, such as the description of Jerusalem's temple and the mention of Sheshonq's campaign, could not have been invented in the seventh century or later.
For the most part, the angels sent by Go: For the most part, the angels sent by God to intervene in men's lives appeared to them in human form (Gn 18.2; 19.1; Dn 8.15).
Foreign gods are called shedim (Deut. 32: Foreign gods are called shedim (Deut. 32:17; Ps. 106:37; cf. i Cor. 10:20), rendered "demons" or "devils" in most translations. The word is related to Akkadian šêdu ("demon"; good or evil).
Furthermore, if historical, Luke’s accou: Furthermore, if historical, Luke’s account would contradict Matthew’s clear indication that Jesus was born shortly before the death of Herod I (that is, around a decade earlier, in 6 B.C.E.). Attempts to suggest that Luke’s reference to the “first registration” (Luke 2:2) was an earlier census carried out by Quirinius have not been successful.
Gen 1 occurs over seven days, and the En: Gen 1 occurs over seven days, and the Enuma Elish is told across seven tablets. On the sixth day God creates humans, which Marduk does in the sixth tablet of the Enuma Elish.
Genesis 1 is formalized, it's highly str: Genesis 1 is formalized, it's highly structured, it has the seven days and everything's paired up. It's beautifully structured, it's very abstract. Genesis 2 is much more dramatic, much more earthy.
Genesis 1 refers to God, as in your tran: Genesis 1 refers to God, as in your translation "God," Elohim, the word that's translated as "God." He's remote, he's transcendent. He creates effortlessly through his word and through his will.
Genesis 1 speaks of male and female, one: Genesis 1 speaks of male and female, one set of Hebrew terms, but Genesis 2 uses man and woman, a different set of Hebrew terms to describe the genders.
Genesis 1, the first creation account, i: Genesis 1, the first creation account, is attributed to P.
Genesis 1:2 says that darkness was on th: Genesis 1:2 says that darkness was on the face of the deep, and the Hebrew word, tehom, has no definite article. Hayes says it is etymologically the same word as Tiamat, the feminine ending aside, and Paul's entry calls the two etymological equivalents. The NABRE's notes call the abyss the primordial ocean of ancient Semitic cosmogony, and read verse 2 as the chaos out of which God brings order. With the wind of God sweeping over the waters, Hayes argues, the storyteller sets the stage for the cosmic battle that everyone knew, and then tells no battle: the elements are there, but demythologized, and God imposes order on water that is just water. The Coogan and Chapman summary likewise gives the demythologizing of the battle before creation as an example of how Genesis transforms Near Eastern myth. Paul draws the same contrast: Tiamat is a primal generative force, while tehom is merely a poetic term for a lifeless mass of water. Hayes and Paul both note that biblical poetry elsewhere alludes to the older story of a battle with a sea monster, and that Genesis 1 pointedly leaves it out; Paul reads the mention of “the great sea monsters” in Genesis 1:21 as most likely part of that polemic.
Got Questions Ministries, an evangelical: Got Questions Ministries, an evangelical ministry, says the book identifies the prophet Daniel as its author and was likely written between 540 and 530 BCE; another of its pages puts it between 536 and 530 BCE, near the end of his captivity. Ligonier Ministries' Reformation Study Bible says certain details in Daniel 11:36–12:3 cannot be harmonized with the death of Antiochus IV, and that for this reason some interpreters read those verses as describing the Antichrist.
Hayes counts Goliath being killed twice,: Hayes counts Goliath being killed twice, once by David and once by another hero, among the duplicates scholars take as evidence that 1 Samuel combines conflicting sources, and Carol Meyers's and Keith Bodner's Bible Odyssey articles name the same tension. The Encyclopaedia Judaica and the notes of the New American Bible say the author of Chronicles resolved the contradiction by having Elhanan kill Lahmi, the brother of Goliath. The HarperCollins Bible Dictionary reports that some interpreters think the oldest tradition did not name David's opponent and that the name of Elhanan's victim was later given to him. The Encyclopaedia Judaica says some scholars hold Elhanan was David's original name, but judges it more likely that Elhanan's exploit was transferred to the more famous David. The NABRE notes say 1 Samuel 16–17 holds two traditions of how David entered Saul's service, of which the Greek translation keeps only one. Sandie Gravett's Bible Odyssey article says more critical readers recognise the tale as apocryphal, and the Encyclopaedia Judaica reports Alexander Rofé's argument for a post-exilic date. Moshe Garsiel argues that, despite its legendary elements and textual problems, the general reality of the story of the duel should prevail.
Hayes says creation in Genesis 1 is not: Hayes says creation in Genesis 1 is not described as making something out of utter nothing, creation ex nihilo, but as organizing pre-existing materials and imposing order on them: when God begins, something already exists, without shape. The Coogan and Chapman summary says that in this account God does not create the universe out of nothing, and that the cosmos was formed out of untamed, though preexisting, matter; it counts the formation of the cosmos out of existing matter, in Enuma Elish Tiamat's body, among the account's affinities with the Babylonian epic. Paul's entry says the verb in the first sentence does not imply creation out of nothing, as most traditional commentators believed, but denotes, as it does throughout the Bible, a divine activity that is effortlessly effected.
He could have singled out various sins,: He could have singled out various sins, but he chose to take same-sex relations as his example (Rom 1:24-28). It represented both to him and to his readers pagan depravity.
He forms the human like a potter working: He forms the human like a potter working with clay. He talks to himself, he plants a garden, he takes a stroll in the garden in the cool of the evening. He makes clothes for Adam and Eve. He's spoken of in much more anthropomorphic terms then the God that we encounter in Genesis 1.
In Genesis 1, plants and animals are mad: In Genesis 1, plants and animals are made before humans, and male and female are created together; in the second account there are no plants before the man, the animals are made after him, and the woman is formed from his rib, as Paul's entry sets out. Genesis 1 calls the deity Elohim, translated “God”; Genesis 2 calls him Yahweh Elohim, “the LORD God”. Hayes describes Genesis 1 as formal, highly structured and abstract, and Genesis 2 as more dramatic and earthy and full of puns, and the Coogan and Chapman summary says the second account has a different style and theme from the first; the two also use different Hebrew terms for the sexes. In Genesis 1 God is remote and creates effortlessly by word and will; in Genesis 2 he forms the human like a potter, plants a garden and walks in it, and is described in much more anthropomorphic terms. The Coogan and Chapman summary adds that the accounts give different reasons for making humans: in the first, to have dominion over the earth; in the second, to till and keep the garden. Paul cautions that the first account, though more hymnlike, does not reflect a completely abstract, transcendent conception of God, as is usually assumed.
In Genesis 1.1–2.4a God is a distant or: In Genesis 1.1–2.4a God is a distant or remote figure who can produce just by speaking. The God of Genesis 2.4b–3.24 is more accessible and anthropomorphic.
In Genesis 1:30, God says that the anima: In Genesis 1:30, God says that the animals are being given the green plants, the grass and herbs, for food.
In Genesis 3 we meet the cunning serpent: In Genesis 3 we meet the cunning serpent, and although many later Hellenistic Jewish texts and the New Testament will identify the snake as a Satan, an enticer, a tempter, some sort of evil creature, he doesn't seem to be so in this fable. There's no real devil or Satan character — we'll talk about Job later — in the Hebrew Bible, the snake in Eden is simply a talking animal.
In Rom 1:26-27, Paul does seem to expres: In Rom 1:26-27, Paul does seem to express the view that homosexual behavior on the part of both men and women is unnatural. He did not, of course, have access to the scientific evidence that we have today, and his main point is to denounce idolatry. His comments on sex in Rom 1 are part of his strategy for condemning idol worship.
In a few cases a Qumran reading is clear: In a few cases a Qumran reading is clearly superior to the mt: thus, for example, 4qdtq reads for Deuteronomy 32:8 bny'l, as does the lxx, instead of bny ysr'l of the mt.
In addition, among the Dead Sea Scrolls: In addition, among the Dead Sea Scrolls at Qumran were found the Prayer of Nabonidus and Tales of the Persian Court. The former, concerning an unnamed Jewish exorcist, is similar to Dan 1-6
In conclusion, I propose to interpret Le: In conclusion, I propose to interpret Lev. 18:22 (and 20:13) as a prohibition of male-male intercourse with a married man.
In that narrative, the outline matches t: In that narrative, the outline matches the outline that we have in Genesis 6-9 where the flood hero is warned of this decision that the gods make to wipe out the earth by a flood.
In the Hebrew Scriptures, there is only: In the Hebrew Scriptures, there is only one clear reference to Lilith. Isaiah 34:14, describing the devastation of Edom, maintains that Lilith shall be at rest in the desert, among wild animals, screech owls, and satyrs. This reference to Lilith as demon is more fully developed in postbiblical Jewish literature
In the classic Documentary Hypothesis, a: In the classic Documentary Hypothesis, as Hayes presents it, source critics dated J to about the tenth century BCE, perhaps the time of Solomon, because the borders of the land God promises to Israel's ancestors match those of David and Solomon's kingdom, and they took it to be a document from Judah, the southern kingdom. Julius Wellhausen dated P to the exile that followed the fall of the southern kingdom in 586 BCE or after it, and source critics saw priestly writers as the final editors who brought the older sources together. Hayes calls Wellhausen's dating of P one of his most controversial points, still hotly debated, and says it owes a great deal to his biases and religious ideology. Of Genesis 1 in particular she says it was added to the Pentateuch probably in one of the last rounds of editing, probably in the sixth century, though “we don't really know”. The Coogan and Chapman summary reports that scholars have found fault with the hypothesis's dating of the sources and with its number of sources.
In the first account in Genesis 1, the c: In the first account in Genesis 1, the creation of the human is clearly the climactic divine act
It is applied frequently to human agents: It is applied frequently to human agents (e.g., Gen. 32:4) and is sometimes used figuratively (e.g., Ps. 104:4). This term was rendered in the Greek Bible by angelos which has the same variety of meanings; only when it was borrowed by the Latin Bible and then passed into other European languages did it acquire the exclusive meaning of "angel."
It places King Ahaziahu (and his father,: It places King Ahaziahu (and his father, Jehoram), who according to Kings reigned only one year (2 Kgs 8:28–29), in precisely the same chronological and historical context as portrayed in Kings: at the Battle of Ramoth-Gilead, where he fought side by side with the last Omride king of Israel, Joram son of Ahab.
Jan Joosten says Leviticus mentions only: Jan Joosten says Leviticus mentions only male-male intercourse and that the Hebrew Bible has nothing to say about female same-sex relations; J. Stiebert and Carol Anderson's entry in the Encyclopedia of Religion say the same. Robert Kawashima's Bible Odyssey word study suggests this may be because, in such encounters, no one's masculinity is at risk. Lee Jefferson's Bible Odyssey article says the absence has led commentators to argue that the authors were fixated on male nonprocreative intercourse. David Instone-Brewer cautions that the lists in Leviticus are not exhaustive, so it is unsafe to base conclusions on the absence. The HarperCollins Bible Dictionary calls Romans 1:26–27 the only biblical reference to female homosexuality. William Loader's Bible Odyssey article reads Romans 1:26 as about same-sex relationships between women, while noting that some scholars read “unnatural” relations there as birth control or nonprocreative sex between men and women.
Jeffrey Geoghegan's Bible Odyssey articl: Jeffrey Geoghegan's Bible Odyssey article says the biblical account seems to be the product of at least two distinct traditions that were later woven into a single narrative, and that the number and character of its differences have led most scholars to that conclusion. The New Catholic Encyclopedia entry says that for more than two centuries scholars have recognized distinguishable sources in the Pentateuch, and that in the flood account at least two were woven together, often called the Yahwist source (J) and the Priestly source (P). Christine Hayes's Yale lecture likewise finds two flood stories in Genesis 6–9 with distinctive styles, themes, vocabularies and details, interwoven rather than placed side by side as the two creation stories are, and the chapter summary for Coogan and Chapman's textbook says that in Genesis 6.5–9.17 the J and P sources, which until then appear separately, are interconnected and woven together. The Encyclopaedia Judaica entry says the story developed in more than a single tradition and that the strands were carefully interwoven without eliminating some contradictions and duplications. The sources give their reasons. The story tells things twice and the tellings disagree: Noah is told to bring two of every kind of animal in one place and seven pairs of clean animals and one pair of unclean in another; the flood lasts 40 days in one verse and 150 in another; and some passages name God Yahweh (“the LORD”) and others Elohim (“God”). Geoghegan notes that earlier interpreters reconciled these differences one by one, as phases of the flood or as an expanded command, and allows that this may be; it is their number and character, here and in many other duplicate stories, that persuades most scholars. On this reading the seven pairs of clean animals belong to the tradition in which Noah offers a sacrifice after the flood, and the other tradition, often associated with priestly interests, has no such sacrifice, since sacrifice is the domain of priests. The New Catholic Encyclopedia adds that when the J elements are taken out, the P parts form a complete and consistent narrative.
Jennifer Knust's Bible Odyssey word stud: Jennifer Knust's Bible Odyssey word study says Paul is the first writer in Greek literature to use arsenokoitai, which makes it hard to translate. One proposal is that the Septuagint wording of Leviticus 18:22 and 20:13 inspired the coinage; she finds neither leading explanation satisfactory and says scholars remain divided, and notes that the NRSVue renders it “men who engage in illicit sex” with a footnote that the meaning of the Greek is uncertain. The HarperCollins Bible Dictionary says the noun after “adulterers” in 1 Corinthians 6:9 literally means “soft”, a word sometimes used of the passive partner in sex between men, and that the next word means one who lies with a male, taking the active role; William Loader's Bible Odyssey article gives the same reading with a “probably”. Jimmy Hoke's Bible Odyssey article says scholars disagree on exactly what these terms refer to, and Bruce Wells's says scholars debate whether Paul means primarily pederasty or all homosexual behavior.
Jesus and the Gospel writers present Sat: Jesus and the Gospel writers present Satan as Jesus's declared personal adversary (Mark 3:23; Luke 11:18–21), paralleling the representation of Satan as Yahweh's adversary in Jewish apocrypha
Jesus’s first miracle in the Gospel of M: Jesus’s first miracle in the Gospel of Mark, for example, is an exorcism in a Capernaum synagogue (Mark 1:21–28).
John Bowker's Concise Oxford Dictionary: John Bowker's Concise Oxford Dictionary of World Religions says Lucifer, Latin for “light-bringer”, is an epithet for the king of Babylon in the Vulgate and King James Version of Isaiah 14:12, and that some of the church fathers, reading it with Luke 10:18, took it as a name for the devil, so that Isaiah 14:12–16 became one basis for the idea that the devil is a rebellious angel cast into hell. Laura Quick's article in Vetus Testamentum says the poem is linked to a Babylonian ruler only in a secondary way, by its framing verses, and that hêlēl ben-šaḥar is almost universally understood as the morning star, the planet Venus, the reading behind the Vulgate's Lucifer. Quick herself argues that Venus is not the necessary or even the most obvious reading.
Judges 1 gives a long list of the places: Judges 1 gives a long list of the places from which the Canaanites were not expelled.
Lev. 20:13 parallels 18:22 in form and c: Lev. 20:13 parallels 18:22 in form and content, the main difference being that while 18:22 simply prohibits a specific acts, adding that it is “an abomination,” 20:13 stipulates a punishment.
Lucifer (Lat., ‘light-bringer’). In the: Lucifer (Lat., ‘light-bringer’). In the Vulgate and Authorized Version of Isaiah 14. 12 (‘How art thou fallen from heaven, O Lucifer’), an epithet for the king of Babylon. By some of the fathers it was taken in conjunction with Luke 10. 18 as a name for the devil, so that the whole passage Isaiah 14. 12–16 became one basis for the myth (developed in Milton's Paradise Lost) that the devil is a rebellious angel cast into hell.
Lynn Huber's Bible Odyssey article names: Lynn Huber's Bible Odyssey article names Genesis 19:1–11, Leviticus 18:22 and 20:13, Romans 1:26–28, 1 Corinthians 6:9–10 and 1 Timothy 1:9–10 as a collection of passages commonly called the “clobber passages”. The HarperCollins Bible Dictionary says the most explicit Old Testament references are in the Holiness Code of Leviticus, and that the New Testament contains three references to homosexual practice, two of them in lists of vices. William Loader's Bible Odyssey article says there are very few references in the New Testament, all in writings associated with Paul.
Many scholars have suggested that two of: Many scholars have suggested that two of the Pentateuch's sources, P and E, preserve a memory of a time when Israel worshipped the Canaanite god El. Christine Hayes's Yale lecture points to Exodus 6:2–4, assigned to P, where God tells Moses that he appeared to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob as El Shaddai but did not make himself known to them by his name Yahweh. The J source, by contrast, has the earliest humans worship Yahweh by name from Genesis 4:26. The patriarchs, Hayes says, seem to have worshipped El, and P and E insist that they worshipped God as El and that God revealed himself as Yahweh at the time of the Exodus. The chapter summary for Coogan and Chapman's introductory textbook likewise says Genesis appears to preserve a tradition from the period when Israel's ancestors prayed to El, the Canaanite god worshipped by Israel's neighbors. Its summary of the Exodus chapter notes that the sources all present the God of the ancestors and the God of the Exodus as continuous, but reads God's first revealing himself as Yahweh in Exodus as an echo of change, recalling a time when the Israelites switched their loyalties from the worship of the sky god to the worship of the storm-god.
Marius Nel counts eight copies of the bi: Marius Nel counts eight copies of the biblical book among the Qumran scrolls, and Craig Evans eight fragmentary scrolls. Nel dates 4QDanc to the late second or early first century BCE, closer to its original than any other biblical book among the scrolls. Popović and colleagues' 2025 radiocarbon test gives 4Q114, a copy of Daniel 8–11, a range of 230–160 BCE, which they say makes it one of the first known fragments of a biblical book from the time of its presumed authors. Nel notes that the scrolls preserve the shift from Hebrew to Aramaic at 2:4b and back to Hebrew at 8:1.
More critical readers recognize the apoc: More critical readers recognize the apocryphal nature of this tale. Not only is it one of two accounts of how David came into the service of Saul (the other being as a musician, 1Sam 16:18-23), it also conflicts with 2Sam 21:19, which states that a fighter named Elhanan defeated Goliath in a different battle.
Nevertheless, there are passages where d: Nevertheless, there are passages where demon-like creatures may be implied (see Isa 34:14–15) or where foreign gods may carry demonic valences (see Deut 32:17).
No scholar doubts this event: not only i: No scholar doubts this event: not only is the story found in both Mark and John but the embarrassment felt by the Gospel writers regarding the obvious conundrum of a sinless Jesus’ baptism for the forgiveness of sin (see especially Matt 3:14-15) suggests a long-established tradition.
No wonder that most scholars who dealt w: No wonder that most scholars who dealt with the early history of Israel avoided using the account of 2 Sam 8:1–14 for their historical reconstruction and treated it as late historiographical work that does not reflect the ancient reality.
Nor does it mention Paul by name: instea: Nor does it mention Paul by name: instead, it confronts the challenge he presents—most seriously in his law-free gospel that emphasizes faith in a way that seems to ignore works, hearing, and believing without doing (Jas 1:22-25, Jas 2:14-26).
Omer Sergi’s “Saul, David, and the Forma: Omer Sergi’s “Saul, David, and the Formation of the Israelite Monarchy: Revisiting the Historical and Literary Context of 1 Samuel 9–2 Samuel 5” contests one of the most accepted hypotheses in biblical scholarship, namely, that the biblical traditions about Saul originated in the kingdom of Israel and that they arrived in Judah only after the fall of Samaria (720 BCE) and stimulated the composition of the stories about David’s rise, which are dated, accordingly, to the seventh century BCE.
On a larger scale, the book of Joshua pr: On a larger scale, the book of Joshua proclaims that the Israelites conquered “the whole land” (e.g., Josh 10:40), but the book of Judges describes the survival of many Canaanites and other peoples.
One thing that most people do in fact ag: One thing that most people do in fact agree on is that the oldest account of the event is a poetic fragment that's found in Exodus 15, verses one to 12, in particular.
Only one angel is said to be able to fly: Only one angel is said to be able to fly (Dn 9.21).
Or in 1Sam 17:50, David kills Goliath, w: Or in 1Sam 17:50, David kills Goliath, whereas in 2Sam 21:19, Elhanan does.
Other biblical descriptions of God are m: Other biblical descriptions of God are much more reminiscent of the Canaanite storm-god Baal, who in Canaanite mythology defeated El and took his place as head of the pantheon. Like Baal, Yahweh is said to ride on the clouds, his revelations come with thunderstorms and earthquakes, and poetic fragments allude to his victory over water foes. In the Song of the Sea in Exodus 15, Yahweh is described as a storm-god. Hayes reports Michael Coogan's observation that Baal was the key figure in a change in the religion of Canaan somewhere between 1500 and 1200 BCE, part of a wider pattern in which a younger storm-god takes power from an older god by defeating a water god. Following Coogan, she finds that in Exodus 15 there seems to be a collective memory of a similar change in Israel's religion, in which Yahweh establishes himself as the god of the Israelites in place of El. The chapter summary for Coogan and Chapman's textbook describes a fundamental shift by the end of the Late Bronze Age, in which a younger god, usually identified as a storm-god, supplants an older one.
Other differences include the duration o: Other differences include the duration of the flood (“40 days” in Gen 7:17; “150 days” in Gen 7:24), the number of each animal entering the ark (“two of each” in Gen 6:19; “seven pairs of clean” and “one pair of unclean” in Gen 7:2), and the types of birds sent to determine if dry land has appeared (“a raven” in Gen 8:7; “a dove” three times in Gen 8:8-12).
Other terms—like arsenkoitai and malakoi: Other terms—like arsenkoitai and malakoi in 1Cor 6:9 or para phusin in Rom 1:26–27—seem to refer to specific sexual practices or preferences, but scholars disagree on exactly what those are.
Part of it, “the upper water” (Ps 148:4;: Part of it, “the upper water” (Ps 148:4; Dn 3:60), is held up by the dome of the sky (vv. 6–7), from which rain descends on the earth
Paul is the first writer in Greek litera: Paul is the first writer in Greek literature to employ this term (see also 1 Tim 1:10), which makes it especially challenging to translate.
Paul mentions “male-bedders” and “softie: Paul mentions “male-bedders” and “softies,” probably referring to active and passive male partners (1Cor 6:9-10; see also 1Tim 1:10).
Paul’s concern is not just pederasty but: Paul’s concern is not just pederasty but also consensual sex (Rom 1:27).
Pieter Craffert's article in HTS Teologi: Pieter Craffert's article in HTS Teologiese Studies says the one aspect most historical Jesus scholars agree on is that Jesus was a successful healer and an exorcist of repute, but that there is no agreement on what he did when exorcising demons. Graham Twelftree's Bible Odyssey article says Mark portrays Jesus as a prolific exorcist, that no other figure in antiquity is known for whom exorcism was so important, and that John's Gospel mentions no exorcisms. Travis Proctor's Bible Odyssey article says exorcism is the miracle of Jesus that Mark mentions most often, that Mark's first miracle is an exorcism in the synagogue at Capernaum (Mark 1:21–28), and that the idea that demons could possess bodies and be cast out by ritual experts is found in Jewish texts such as the Dead Sea Scrolls and Josephus.
Satan's evil function in 1 Chr 21.1, the: Satan's evil function in 1 Chr 21.1, then, shows that the Chronicler was aware of a personal principle of evil that warred against God and enticed man to rebel against Him.
Scholars also debate about the kind of s: Scholars also debate about the kind of sexual practice that Paul is referring to in 1Cor 6:9-10. Some have argued it is primarily pederasty (a homosexual relationship between a grown man, often married, and an adolescent boy) and that Paul would not have known about our concept of sexual orientation. Others disagree and say that Paul’s statements do indeed categorize all homosexual behavior as “unrighteous.”
Scholars note a tension between this sto: Scholars note a tension between this story (1Sam 17) and the one in 2Sam 21:19-22, which reports that a certain Elhanan son of Jaare-oregim killed Goliath.
So Israelite accounts of creation contai: So Israelite accounts of creation contain clear allusions to and resonances of Ancient Near Eastern cosmogonies; but perhaps Genesis 1 can best be described as demythologizing what was a common cultural heritage.
So creation in Genesis 1 is not describe: So creation in Genesis 1 is not described as a process of making something out of nothing: that's a notion referred to as creation ex nihilo, creation of something out of utter nothing. It's instead a process of organizing pre-existing materials and imposing order on those chaotic materials.
So in Genesis 2 the deity is Yahweh Eloh: So in Genesis 2 the deity is Yahweh Elohim.
So in the second creation story beginnin: So in the second creation story beginning in Genesis 2:4, we read that the first human is formed when God fashions it from the dust of the earth or clay.
So the main characteristics of the J sou: So the main characteristics of the J source, which begins with the second creation story, so the J source picks up in Genesis 2:4, second half of verse 4 are
So what we have in the first few chapter: So what we have in the first few chapters of Genesis are two creation stories that have distinctive styles, distinctive themes, distinctive vocabularies and they're placed side by side. In Genesis 6 through 9 we seem to have two flood stories with distinctive styles, and themes, and vocabularies, and substantive details, but they're interwoven instead of being placed side by side.
So you have this firmament, which is bea: So you have this firmament, which is beaten back to hold back primeval waters that are pressing in; you have land which is holding down the waters here. We inhabit the bubble that's created in that way. That's the image in Enuma Elish and it's the image of Genesis 1.
So you've got some people reading Romans: So you've got some people reading Romans 1 as a condemnation of modern homosexuality and thinking they're doing a good historical reading of this text. You've got other people who read the same text, using the same methods of historical criticism, and say, are you crazy? He's not talking about homosexuality, that's not his concern.
Some of the latest written texts of the: Some of the latest written texts of the Hebrew Bible start using names for angels, such as Gabriel (Dan 8:16, Dan 9:21) and Michael (Dan 10:13).
T. L. Fallon's entry in the New Catholic: T. L. Fallon's entry in the New Catholic Encyclopedia says the phrase “messenger of the Lord” has a more specific meaning that has not yet been satisfactorily explained: in early texts such as Genesis 16, Exodus 3 and Judges 6 the messenger is presented as God appearing to humans in sensible form. It sets out three theories (the messenger represents God; the messenger is God himself in human form; the messenger was interpolated into older stories of God appearing directly) and says each has valid elements but none solves all the problems. Stephen White's article in the Tyndale Bulletin says it is surprising how little in the literature satisfactorily explains the interchange of the angel and Yahweh, and describes the interpolation theory, which holds that “the angel of the LORD” was added where God's actions seemed too anthropomorphic. Bernard Bamberger's entry in the Encyclopaedia Judaica reports both that some scholars take the angel as a manifestation of the divine power and will and that others suppose later scribes interposed an angel where the earliest stories had God meet a human directly. Benjamin Sommer's Bible Odyssey article reads this mal'akh as a small-scale manifestation of God, part of the deity rather than a separate being.
The Book of Daniel identifies the Prophe: The Book of Daniel identifies the Prophet Daniel as its author (Daniel 9:2; 10:2).
The English transliteration of a Hebrew: The English transliteration of a Hebrew word whose literal meaning is “adversary.” In the OT, the figure of Satan appears only three times (Job 1-2; Zech 3:1-2; 1Chr 21:1).
The Genesis narrative records both attem: The Genesis narrative records both attempted sexual perversity and gross inhospitality (Gen 19:1-11).
The HarperCollins Bible Dictionary calls: The HarperCollins Bible Dictionary calls Romans 1:26–27 the most extensive biblical reference to homosexual acts and says they are mentioned as one example of the perversions that follow when humankind refuses to give glory and thanks to God. William Loader's Bible Odyssey article says Paul chose same-sex relations as his example, and that it represented pagan depravity to him and his readers. Bruce Wells's Bible Odyssey article says Paul does seem to call homosexual behavior by men and women unnatural, but that his main point is to denounce idolatry. On “unnatural”, Loader says that in Paul's world it was unnatural and shameful for a man to take a passive role or a woman an active one, and Jimmy Hoke's Bible Odyssey article says Paul uses the same phrase Roman writers used to associate such practices with foreign deviance. Dale Martin's Yale lectures, on ancient sexual hierarchy generally, say that in ancient Judaism and Christianity it was considered sex “against nature” for a woman to penetrate a man. Loader adds that Paul's concern is not only pederasty but also consensual sex.
The HarperCollins Bible Dictionary says: The HarperCollins Bible Dictionary says satan is a Hebrew word whose literal meaning is “adversary”, and that the figure of Satan appears only three times in the Old Testament, in Job 1–2, Zechariah 3:1–2 and 1 Chronicles 21:1. In the first two, it says, he is a member of God's court whose duty is to accuse human beings before God, and is not presented as an enemy of God or as the leader of the demonic forces of evil. Adam Porter's Bible Odyssey article says that in Job 1–2 the noun has the definite article, “the satan”, and should be translated as a title, “the accuser”, and that the accuser is not responsible for evil in the Hebrew Bible, which generally attributes both good and evil to God. Christine Hayes's Yale lectures call the satan of Job a member of the divine council who acts as a kind of prosecuting attorney, and say he is certainly not the devil: there is no such notion in the Hebrew Bible. The New American Bible's note on Job 1:6 calls the satan a member of the heavenly court, “the accuser”, whom later biblical traditions develop as the devil. Shawna Dolansky's Bible Odyssey talk says “the satan” is a job title, not a proper name. The Encyclopaedia Judaica says the noun is applied to human adversaries, as in 1 Samuel 29:4 and 1 Kings 11:14, and that the angel sent to obstruct Balaam in Numbers 22 was chosen for the occasion, as a satan.

The HarperCollins Bible Dictionary says the Holiness Code of Leviticus prohibits a male, under penalty of death, from lying with another male as a woman does. Christine Hayes's Yale lectures and the chapter summary for Coogan and Chapman's textbook place these chapters in the Holiness Code, a distinct source; Hayes says most scholars think it comes from a different priestly school, designated H, and that Leviticus 18 and 20 list sexual transgressions that defile the land, which will vomit out those who dwell on it. Jan Joosten says 20:13 parallels 18:22 and adds a punishment, and that the verse unambiguously addresses sex between males and has widely been interpreted as a blanket prohibition; he reports Saul Olyan's view that the law was originally aimed at the insertive partner, and proposes his own reading, a prohibition of intercourse with a married man. J. Stiebert says what the phrase means, and how far it reaches, is elusive. Bruce Wells's Bible Odyssey article says that in his opinion no one really knows what “the beds of a woman” means and that most scholars have long read it as the act of lying down, a reading he doubts while saying he is in the minority. David Instone-Brewer's article in HIPHIL Novum argues that it is no longer certain that Leviticus condemned all homoerotic activity.
The Hebrew term mal’akh, like the Greek: The Hebrew term mal’akh, like the Greek term angelos, means “messenger.” The Hebrew Bible uses the term on rare occasion when speaking of a human messenger (Gen 32:3), but typically the term refers to heavenly beings who serve what the Bible regards as the one true God, Yhwh.
The LXX text of Ps 16:10 does differ fro: The LXX text of Ps 16:10 does differ from the standard Masoretic Text (MT) of the Hebrew, but recent gains in textual criticism demonstrate that we can no longer say whether the LXX or the MT represents a “more original” text, if we can even speak of such a thing.
The NABRE introduction says the book was: The NABRE introduction says the book was composed during the persecution carried on by Antiochus IV Epiphanes (167–164 BCE). Christine Hayes's Yale lectures date chapters 7–12 to between 167 and 164 BCE, and the first six chapters perhaps to the end of the third century. Amy Merrill Willis's Bible Odyssey article says the vision of Daniel 8 was written around 167 BCE and that the book's calculations for the end refer to events of 167–164 BCE; its “Did You Know?” box says the Hebrew-Aramaic edition was completed around 163 BCE. The publisher's summary of Coogan and Chapman's introduction says the book was written in the second century BCE, and that scholars place it there. Craig Evans says the dangers Jews faced in the second century BCE, especially under Antiochus IV, led to the writing of the book soon after. Mladen Popović and colleagues note that scholars date Daniel 8–11 on literary-historical grounds to the 160s BCE. The date is not unanimous. Benjamin Suchard writes that the dating has long been a controversial issue, and that the book's sixth-century setting was traditionally taken as its date of composition. The “Did You Know?” box on David Valeta's Bible Odyssey article says scholars debate the date, from as early as the sixth century BCE to as late as the second, and that both viewpoints have strong defenders.
The New Catholic Encyclopedia entry give: The New Catholic Encyclopedia entry gives the ark's dimensions in Genesis 6:15–16, reckoning a cubit at 1.5 feet, as about 450 feet long, 75 feet wide and 45 feet high, with three decks, a roof and a door in its side. It assigns the precise measurements to the Priestly source; Geoghegan says they seem to derive from the passages that call God Elohim. Utnapishtim's boat in Gilgamesh is quite different: the Encyclopaedia Judaica entry calls it a perfect cube of 120 cubits with seven levels, and the New Catholic Encyclopedia puts it at 180 feet on each side. The Encyclopaedia Judaica entry also notes that the Mesopotamian hero needed a boatman to steer, while Noah's vessel had neither rudder nor sail, and reads the building of an ark rather than a ship as crediting Noah's survival to God alone and not to human skill.
The Numbers chapter summary for Coogan a: The Numbers chapter summary for Coogan and Chapman's introductory textbook treats the count of men leaving Egypt in Exodus 12:37 as an example of how the biblical writers often inflated census statistics, and calls the population statistics in the censuses of Numbers likewise unrealistically high. It says no reasonable interpretation for this inflation has ever been presented, though P, the Priestly writer, may have incorporated numbers from a variety of sources to show that the divine promise of descendants had been fulfilled. The summary of the Exodus chapter describes the Exodus as a migration not of thousands or millions of people but of a few hundred. The Encyclopaedia Judaica's article on Numbers calls 600,000 a schematic number.
The Septuagint phrasing of Lev 18:22 and: The Septuagint phrasing of Lev 18:22 and Lev 20:13 inspired Paul (or someone else) to coin the term.
The Watchers almost certainly have some: The Watchers almost certainly have some connection to the sons of God mentioned in Gen 6:1–13
The accuser is not responsible for evil: The accuser is not responsible for evil in the Hebrew Bible; rather the Hebrew Bible generally attributes both good and evil to God (1Sam 18:10, 1Kgs 22, etc.).
The angel who was sent to obstruct Balaa: The angel who was sent to obstruct Balaam (Num. 22:32) was evidently chosen ad hoc, as a satan
The battle of the Elah Valley and the du: The battle of the Elah Valley and the duel between David and Goliath (2 Samuel 17) have been analyzed from different points of view. But the assessment about the validity of the general reality of the story should prevail, despite the legendary elements and textual problems.
The biblical account of the latter years: The biblical account of the latter years of Saul’s reign (1Sam 16:14-31:13) presents him mainly as a foil against which David’s rise to power appears all the more glorious.
The manuscript preserves Daniel 8–11, wh: The manuscript preserves Daniel 8–11, which scholars date on literary-historical grounds to the 160s BCE
The most explicit OT references to such: The most explicit OT references to such a practice are in the Holiness Code of Leviticus, where, under penalty of death, a male is strictly prohibited from lying with another male as a woman does (Lev 18:22; Lev 20:13).
The most extensive biblical reference to: The most extensive biblical reference to homosexual acts (and the only biblical reference to female homosexuality) is in (Rom 1:26-27).
The name for this watery abyss, part of: The name for this watery abyss, part of which is personified by the goddess Tiamat, is the etymological equivalent of the Hebrew tehom (Gen. 1:2), a proper name that always appears in the Bible without the definite article.
The name occurs in the Bible (i Chron. 2: The name occurs in the Bible (i Chron. 26:7) but not yet as an angelic name, first appearing as such in the Apocrypha (Tob. 12:15 and i En. 20:3), where he is one of the seven archangels.
The noun listed after “adulterers” in (1: The noun listed after “adulterers” in (1Cor 6:9) literally means “soft” and was sometimes applied in Greek literature to a male who was the passive partner during homosexual intercourse. The following word in that list literally means “a person [probably a male person] who lies with a male,” that is, one who takes the active role in homosexual intercourse.
The noun “satan” appears in the Hebrew B: The noun “satan” appears in the Hebrew Bible as a name (“Satan”) only in 1Chr 21:1.

The noun “satan” appears in the Hebrew Bible as a name (“Satan”) only in 1Chr 21:1. In the longest story involving him (Job 1-2), the noun has a definite article (“the satan”) and should be translated as a title (“the accuser”).
The opening sentence in the story – many: The opening sentence in the story – many commentators think (but see Cassuto, Genesis, 1, pp. 19–20) – begins with a temporal clause, "When God began to create the heaven and the earth" (Gen. 1:1), continues with a circumstantial clause telling of the existence of the darkness and void (1:2)
The satan: lit., “adversary” (as in 1 Kg: The satan: lit., “adversary” (as in 1 Kgs 11:14). Here a member of the heavenly court, “the accuser” (Zec 3:1). In later biblical traditions this character will be developed as the devil (Gk. diabolos, “adversary”).
The snake was identified with the devil: The snake was identified with the devil (Wis 2:24; Jn 8:44; Rev 12:9; 20:2), whose eventual defeat seemed implied in the verse.
The three that I've listed here are the: The three that I've listed here are the biggies: idolatry, homicide and sexual transgressions. These are spelled out in Leviticus 18 and Leviticus 20, those two chapters.
The “pharaoh of the exodus” (Exod 5-12),: The “pharaoh of the exodus” (Exod 5-12), often identified by biblical scholars as Rameses II (1279–1212 BCE) or, somewhat less likely, his son and successor, Merenptah (1212–1202 BCE).
There are several other creation myths f: There are several other creation myths from the Near East that bear striking similarities to the Genesis narratives, including the Babylonian myth Enuma Elish, which shares a number of affinities with Genesis 1.
There are some passages in which the flo: There are some passages in which the flood is said to have lasted for 40 days, or be on the earth for 40 days. We find that in Genesis 7:17, but in Genesis 7:24, 150 days is given as the time of the flood.
There, such activity is mentioned as one: There, such activity is mentioned as one example of the perversions that follow when humankind refuses to give glory and thanks to the one sovereign God (Rom 1:18-25; Rom 1:28-32).
Therefore, humans, according to Genesis: Therefore, humans, according to Genesis 1, were created vegetarian, and in every respect, the original creation is imagined as free of bloodshed and violence of every kind.
These books include independent blocks (: These books include independent blocks (e.g., the Ark Narrative [1 Sm 4:1–7:1], Saul’s rise to power [1 Sm 9:1–11:15], David’s ascendancy over Saul [1 Sm 16–31], the Succession Narrative [2 Sm 9–20; 1 Kgs 1–2]), which the editor shaped into three narrative cycles, the last two marked by transitional passages in 1 Sm 13:1 and 2 Sm 1:1.
This chapter also shows how the Flood na: This chapter also shows how the Flood narratives, like the creation myths in Genesis 1–3, borrow heavily from the antecedent Flood narratives of Israel’s Near Eastern neighbors.
This imperial history is reflected in th: This imperial history is reflected in the pages of the Bible itself, where certain texts were actually composed in Aramaic, including Gen 31:47, Jer 10:11, Ezra 4:8-6:18, Ezra 7:12-26, and Dan 2:4b-7:28.
Thus, those passages employing the divin: Thus, those passages employing the divine name “God” (Hebrew ‘elohim) present a deity who is transcendent and systematic in carrying out the flood. The precise measurements of the ark (Gen 6:14-15), the age of Noah before and after the flood (Gen 7:11; Gen 8:13), and the recurring references to specific days, months and years (Gen 8:4-5, Gen 8:13-14), all seem to derive from this source.
Travis Proctor's Bible Odyssey article o: Travis Proctor's Bible Odyssey article on demons says the most common account among ancient Jews and Christians made demons the spirits of primordial giants born of fallen angels and mortal women, a narrative found in the Book of the Watchers. McKenna Boling and Travis Proctor's article on the Watchers dates that book to the third or second century BCE, says its Watchers almost certainly have some connection to the sons of God of Genesis 6, and cites 1 Enoch 15:9–12 for the giants' souls tormenting the earth as demonic beings after their death. Joseph Angel's Bible Odyssey article says the Book of the Watchers makes the biblical sons of God rebellious angels, says parts of it date as early as the fourth century BCE, and notes that in some versions the giants' disembodied spirits survive as demonic forces. Walter Stephens's entry in the Encyclopedia of Religion says pseudepigraphic and Talmudic sources identify some demons as the souls of the dead giants. Bernard Bamberger's entry on the Nephilim in the Encyclopaedia Judaica says Second Temple writings elaborated and reinterpreted the fragmentary narrative of Genesis 6, making the angels rebels against God and their giant offspring wicked, ideas it says are not in the biblical text. Kelley Coblentz Bautch's Bible Odyssey article says many scholars think 2 Peter 2:4 and Jude 6 allude to the punishment of fallen angels in the Enoch literature, and that Jude 14–15 quotes the Book of the Watchers.
Travis Proctor's Bible Odyssey article s: Travis Proctor's Bible Odyssey article says the Hebrew Bible has relatively little to say about demons proper, that the Greek term has no direct equivalent in Hebrew, and that the Septuagint uses “demon” mainly for foreign gods; demon-like creatures may be implied in Isaiah 34:14–15, and foreign gods may carry demonic overtones in Deuteronomy 32:17. L. F. Hartman's entry in the New Catholic Encyclopedia says demonology played an insignificant role in the older books of the Old Testament, though belief in demons was widespread in the ancient Near East. Delbert Hillers's entry in the Encyclopaedia Judaica says the Bible's foreign gods are called shedim, a word related to Akkadian šêdu, and warns against overestimating the small traces of belief in demons in the Bible or underestimating the difficulty of interpreting them, since it is often impossible to tell whether a named demon belonged to living belief or to literary language. Rebecca Lesses's entry in the Encyclopedia of Religion says Isaiah 34:14 is the only clear reference to Lilith in the Hebrew Scriptures, and that Lilith as a demon is developed in later Jewish literature. Liane Feldman's Bible Odyssey article says Azazel, to whom the scapegoat is sent in Leviticus 16, remains somewhat enigmatic, and has been identified as a place, a foreign deity or a wilderness demon.
